lead: A quantum computer with many qubits is described by one state vector, and that vector is built from smaller spaces. The tensor product V ⊗ W does the building: it produces a space whose dimension is the product of the two dimensions, with basis vectors written |ij⟩. A gate that acts on one qubit at a time is a matrix formed by the Kronecker product; a gate that acts on several qubits jointly, such as CNOT, is a general 4×4 unitary that need not be any single Kronecker product. Every circuit is a walk through this larger space. This chapter defines the construction, gives the product basis of two qubits, and shows how operators combine.
prereq: You need: 1.2 for complex vector spaces, 1.3 for bases and Dirac notation, and 1.4 for operators written as matrices.

blocks.text: Two quantum systems described together need one state vector, not two. That vector lives in a space built from the two separate spaces by the tensor product, written V ⊗ W.

Let V be a complex vector space of dimension m and W one of dimension n, where the dimension is the number of vectors in a basis. The tensor product V ⊗ W is a new complex vector space. It is spanned by symbols |v⟩ ⊗ |w⟩, one for every pair of vectors, and the symbol is linear in each slot separately. That rule is called bilinearity.

blocks.where: α is a complex number, |v⟩ is a vector in V, |w⟩ is a vector in W. A scalar may sit on either side of the ⊗ or outside the bracket.
the same rule holds in the second slot; with the scalar rule, this is bilinearity.

blocks.text: Bilinearity is the whole point. It says amplitudes multiply rather than add: (2|v⟩) ⊗ |w⟩ is 2(|v⟩ ⊗ |w⟩). Quantum mechanics needs exactly this, because a joint amplitude is the product of the two single-system amplitudes, and a sum inside one slot must spread across the joint state.
Dimension follows from the bases. If |0⟩,…,|m−1⟩ is a basis of V and |0⟩,…,|n−1⟩ is a basis of W, the mn vectors |i⟩ ⊗ |j⟩ form a basis of V ⊗ W.
dim(V ⊗ W) = dim V × dim W = m·n
blocks.where: dim V is the number of basis vectors of V, dim W is the number for W, so the product space has dimension mn (a single number).

blocks.text: So two qubits live in C² ⊗ C², of dimension 2 × 2 = 4, and three qubits in a space of dimension 8. Each extra qubit doubles the number of amplitudes. That doubling is the source of both the power and the cost of quantum computing.

sections.h3: The product basis and the |ij⟩ shorthand

blocks.text: We shorten |i⟩ ⊗ |j⟩ to |ij⟩. In C² ⊗ C² the four basis vectors are |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩. The left symbol is the first qubit, the right symbol the second.
A general vector is a complex combination of all mn product basis vectors.

blocks.where: c<sub>ij</sub> is the complex amplitude of the basis vector |ij⟩, and the double sum runs over all mn pairs.

blocks.text: For two qubits this reads |Ψ⟩ = c<sub>00</sub>|00⟩ + c<sub>01</sub>|01⟩ + c<sub>10</sub>|10⟩ + c<sub>11</sub>|11⟩: four complex amplitudes in place of the two that one qubit needs.

blocks.where: δ is 1 when the two indices are equal and 0 otherwise, so the product basis is orthonormal whenever the factor bases are. A physical state then needs Σ|c<sub>ij</sub>|² = 1.

blocks.text: Most vectors in V ⊗ W are not of the form |v⟩ ⊗ |w⟩. The joint state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 is the standard example: no single choice of |v⟩ and |w⟩ reproduces it. Such states are called entangled; Unit 2, Composite systems, reduced and mixed states, takes them up.
Let A act on V and B act on W. Their joint operator A ⊗ B acts on product vectors by (A ⊗ B)(|i⟩ ⊗ |j⟩) = (A|i⟩) ⊗ (B|j⟩), and on sums by linearity.

blocks.where: A<sub>ik</sub> is the entry in row i, column k of A; B<sub>jl</sub> is the entry in row j, column l of B. For 2×2 factors this gives a 4×4 matrix.

blocks.text: In matrix language this is the Kronecker product: take A and replace each entry a<sub>ik</sub> by the whole block a<sub>ik</sub>B. Block row i is the first qubit label, block column k is its column index, and inside each block the second qubit is indexed as usual.

A gate on the first qubit alone is A ⊗ I2, where I2 is the 2×2 identity; a gate on the second alone is I2 ⊗ A. These are different 4×4 matrices whenever A is not the identity. For instance X ⊗ I2 sends |00⟩ to |10⟩ and |01⟩ to |11⟩, flipping only the first label. Such matrices are unitary, as 1.5 requires of any gate.

An operator acting on both qubits jointly need not split as A ⊗ B at all; CNOT is the standard case, and multi-qubit gates appear in Unit 3, Quantum Gates and Circuits. What stays true is that operators on different qubits commute: (A ⊗ I<sub>2</sub>)(I<sub>2</sub> ⊗ B) = A ⊗ B = (I<sub>2</sub> ⊗ B)(A ⊗ I<sub>2</sub>).

figure.caption: Each branch multiplies one coefficient of |v⟩ by one coefficient of |w⟩: 0.6 × 0.7071 = 0.4243 on the way to |00⟩. The four leaf values are the four amplitudes of |v⟩ ⊗ |w⟩, a space of dimension 2 × 2 = 4, and their squares add to 1.

spec.aria: A tree multiplies the coefficients of |v⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩ and |w⟩ = 0.7071|0⟩ − 0.7071|1⟩: the 0.6 branch gives amplitudes 0.4243 for |00⟩ and −0.4243 for |01⟩, and the 0.8 branch gives 0.5657 for |10⟩ and −0.5657 for |11⟩.

examples.question: Let |v⟩ = (3/5)|0⟩ + (4/5)|1⟩ and |w⟩ = (1/√2)|0⟩ − (1/√2)|1⟩. Write |v⟩ ⊗ |w⟩ in the product basis |00⟩, |01⟩, |10⟩, |11⟩. Give the four amplitudes, state the dimension of the space, and verify the norm.
steps: A product state has c<sub>ij</sub> = v<sub>i</sub>w<sub>j</sub>, so multiply each pair once.
Dimension: dim(C² ⊗ C²) = 2 × 2 = 4, matching the four amplitudes.
examples.check:
from math import sqrt
v0, v1 = 3/5, 4/5
w0, w1 = 1/sqrt(2), -1/sqrt(2)
c00 = v0*w0
c01 = v0*w1
c10 = v1*w0
c11 = v1*w1
for c in (c00, c01, c10, c11):
    print(round(c, 4))
print(round(c00**2 + c01**2 + c10**2 + c11**2, 4))
print(2*2)

traps: Dimension multiplies, not adds. Three qubits give 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 amplitudes, not 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
Order matters. |0⟩ ⊗ |1⟩ = |01⟩ is a different basis state from |10⟩ = |1⟩ ⊗ |0⟩. The two are not interchangeable.
A ⊗ B is not the ordinary matrix product AB. With 2×2 factors, A ⊗ B is 4×4, while AB stays 2×2 and needs both matrices to act on the same space.
Only a scalar slides across the ⊗: α(|v⟩ ⊗ |w⟩) = (α|v⟩) ⊗ |w⟩ = |v⟩ ⊗ (α|w⟩). A sum in one slot does not slide; it splits into two product terms.
The examiner's favourite: not every two-qubit operator equals A ⊗ B. CNOT is a 4×4 unitary that cannot be written as one Kronecker product.

quiz.q: How many dimensions does C² ⊗ C² have, and what are its basis vectors?
Write |1⟩ ⊗ |0⟩ in shorthand. Is it the same vector as |0⟩ ⊗ |1⟩?
Why is dim(V ⊗ W) the product of the dimensions rather than their sum?
quiz.a: A basis of V ⊗ W is every pair |i⟩ ⊗ |j⟩, giving m × n vectors. The direct sum V ⊕ W has only m + n basis vectors, because it keeps the two lists separate and never forms pairs; it cannot carry the products v<sub>i</sub>w<sub>j</sub> that a joint amplitude needs.

quiz.q: Show that (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2 cannot be written as |v⟩ ⊗ |w⟩.
quiz.a: For a product state c<sub>ij</sub> = v<sub>i</sub>w<sub>j</sub>, so c₀₀c₁₁ − c₀₁c₁₀ = v₀w₀v₁w₁ − v₀w₁v₁w₀ = 0 always. Here c₀₀ = c₁₁ = 1/√2 and c₀₁ = c₁₀ = 0, giving 1/2 − 0 = 1/2 ≠ 0. No product state matches.

quiz.q: Why do A ⊗ I₂ and I₂ ⊗ B commute for any 2×2 A and B?
quiz.a: (A ⊗ I₂)(I₂ ⊗ B) = (AI₂) ⊗ (I₂B) = A ⊗ B, and (I₂ ⊗ B)(A ⊗ I₂) = (I₂A) ⊗ (BI₂) = A ⊗ B. Both products equal A ⊗ B, so the order is irrelevant: the two operators act on different qubits.
0. ⟨01|10⟩ = ⟨0|1⟩⟨1|0⟩ = 0 × 0 = 0, because the product basis is orthonormal.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Kronecker product is standard in numerical linear algebra and signal processing, where it describes separable transforms on images and grids. In machine learning and condensed-matter physics, tensor networks such as matrix product states compress the exponentially large joint vectors of many-body systems (2ⁿ amplitudes for n qubits) so they fit in memory. Quantum chemists use tensor products to build many-electron spaces from one-electron orbitals. Two useful search terms are Kronecker product and matrix product state; the physics that the product space allows is the subject of Unit 2.
